column14: Today, family makeup looks different than they did under the traditional norm. Family-sized housing in Washington, D.C. can be found in apartments, condos, or traditional homes. I believe family-sized housing should include a bedroom for the parent(s) and a bedroom for each child or family member who resides in the dwelling. Additionally, family-sized housing should include shared living space for family activities and adequate, flexible storage space that can adapt to a family’s needs. I also believe family-sized housing should feature child-friendly areas for play, whether that is a yard, shared play area, or nearby access to parks. This aspect of home life is critical to children’s development and a family’s overall connection to their community.

Since COVID-19, we have seen a rise in the number of condominiums and apartment buildings being built in our SMD, which has changed the landscape of the neighborhood and raised concerns among some residents about whether we have the transportation and other resources needed to support further development. I am not for building more housing in my immediate SMD today, but I would support additional housing elsewhere in the ANC (4D). column34: I frequently visit the Aldi near Fort Totten for weekly grocery trips. I’ve often driven because it has a parking garage, but I recently mapped out a walkable route from my home. Walking there provides another vantage point to better understand how the community is developing. Moving forward, I commit to doing more grocery trips on foot, along with increasing my walks and use of the bus to get to and from the Fort Totten Metro Station.
column35: One of the biggest issues in my neighborhood is ensuring we see equitable development across our SMD. During recent conversations with neighbors, several expressed concerns about the growth of development along Kennedy Street, fueled by investment from wealthy developers that can limit locals’ ability to invest in and grow their own businesses right at home. Additionally, neighbors do not feel they have an adequate say in weighing in on what businesses or housing types are being added to their neighborhood. I believe that development is only beneficial if it is co-created by the people who will be most impacted by it. The city needs to provide residents with grants or financing programs that can make starting businesses in our communities more accessible. When it comes to community involvement, ANCs need to have a more vocal presence in the neighborhood and communicate changes and opportunities for community input to neighbors in various ways, ensuring they have meaningful opportunities to voice their unique desires for change.  If elected, I would support prioritizing local business development and advocate for our councilmember and the new mayor to conduct more analysis on the number of D.C. small-business owners by SMD and work with ANCs to provide more input on the programs, outreach, and training residents need to turn their ideas into tangible business opportunities. We should also help residents understand how to turn their existing networks into avenues for economic growth and ensure everyone understands how they can contribute to the neighborhood’s economic and overall well-being.
column36: Democracy on paper is a noun, but in reality, it is a verb. During my campaign, I have expanded my outreach beyond traditional media to meet neighbors where they are. This includes creating flyers, doing multiple rounds of door-knocking, providing a campaign phone number, and developing a website where neighbors can learn more about my work and ideas for Brightwood Park. In conversations with neighbors, I have reminded them that I take daily walks around the SMD and encourage folks to say hello or share ideas if they see me walking. If elected, I would continue to use online media, including social media, when possible, to share resources and ways folks can get involved. I would also share news through WhatsApp groups and Nextdoor.com posts, given that neighbors have stated these are other ways they would like to see their ANC connect with constituents. Additionally, I would encourage people to stop me if they see me so we can preserve the supportive environment we’ve created in Brightwood Park and ensure people understand that their ANC is a neighbor who wants to work alongside them to make a difference.
column37: I have been a District resident for 10 years, and throughout my time here, I have worked tirelessly to be a supportive community member. I began my career in the District, serving as a public-school teacher for five years, including two years at Capital City Public Charter School right here in Ward 4, where I taught 8th-grade humanities to students from our community during the COVID-19 pandemic. After my time in the classroom, I served in the United States Senate as an education and workforce policy advisor. I later took those learnings into public-sector consulting, where I have worked with government leaders across the country to expand childcare options for working families, improve teacher pay, and strengthen community programs addressing housing affordability for economically vulnerable residents. Today, I run a public-sector consulting business based in Brightwood Park and continue to serve local families as a member of the Board of Directors for Latin American Montessori Bilingual Public Charter School (LAMB PCS). I have a proven track record of putting my community first, and I know that I can continue to be a force for meaningful change in my SMD if elected as our next ANC.

There will likely be circumstances when these issues arise where I'll have no choice but to vote according to my conscience, and do my best to empathetically hear the perspectives of neighbors with whom I disagree.

column12: I decided on only one option for each of these because I think there has been too much of a  conflation of capital “A” Affordable and lower-case “a” affordable. “Affordable” was the euphemism to replace “subsidized” because of the connotation, but has become many different things to many different people. A market-rate unit can be “affordable” but not “Affordable.” $3,000/month for a 2 bedroom is “affordable” for the DC median household (approx. ⅓ of $107,000/year) but not what many would colloquially consider “affordable.” Saying a developer is building a 10-unit building with an “affordable” unit makes it sound like the unit is being begrudgingly provided by the developer out of their profit instead of a “Affordable” unit being paid for by increasing the costs of the other nine. Many people wonder then mistakenly why all the units cannot be “affordable,” and blame nebulous greed instead of real material conditions.

column35: The sheer inability to afford to live here long-term. The cheapest properties are a few recently built condos that go for $900,000 and single-family homes that exist are $5 million or more. People are always moving out because they cannot afford to start a family and stay here. The businesses have frequent turnover because the few people who do live here are not enough to provide the revenue for them to pay astronomical commercial rents. There are years-long empty commercial buildings such as the old Target in the strip mall, the Uptown and adjoining buildings, the old Yenching restaurant, and numerous shopfronts are vacant without a sizeable customer base. The grocery stores are available but boutique, requiring a trip to Van Ness or further up the Red Line for a full grocery store like Giant or Wegman’s. The neighborhood is also dominated by six-lane Connecticut Ave, making it unwelcome for people to spend time in the neighborhood and difficult to enjoy being out and about.  Seek to make Cleveland Park a more welcoming and desirable place to live. I want to hold more  events that bring the community out like Cleveland Park Day, something like the Dupont Circle Farmer’s Market to support local businesses. I support more car-free street events and think that something like that would be perfect between Cleveland Park and the Zoo. I would push for the adoption of ZC 25-09 to upzone Cleveland Park, and to go beyond that in the future. I will endeavor to make safety a priority for DDOT with the installation of speed bumps on Porter St, and to fix the intersection of Porter and Connecticut that encourages reckless behavior. I want a bus lane to be on Connecticut Ave for the riders of the D70, and I want to resurrect the Connecticut Ave bike lane.
column36: To anyone that I have spoken with, I have been upfront and honest about what I think would make Cleveland Park and my SMD better. Many people disagree, and I will hear out the concerns that people have, and I will try to work with them where possible. But I will not back down in my hope for a better Cleveland Park. I believe in bus lanes, bike lanes, and denser housing, and I believe they make a neighborhood more affordable, safer, and walkable for children and adults of all ages.
column37: I love DC, and I have loved living in Cleveland Park. I think this neighborhood has been allowed to stagnate and become an afterthought in DC despite its rich history, easy transit access, and diverse amenities. I am optimistic about the future, and I think that Cleveland Park can bloom into the envy of the city. That, however, needs Commissioners willing to put in the time and effort to unravel the suffocating patchwork of rules and laws that have been passed specifically to stop any change in the area for the past almost 40 years. I think I am someone with the energy and vision to make that happen. We are more than a six-lane highway and a historical plaque, Cleveland Park is thousands of Washingtonians who love their city and their corner of it and want to make it better. It is a neighborhood that could rival any in the District, and I want to be there to make it happen.
column38: As someone who rides the bus and metro every day, has walked all over the city, and occasionally been known to bike, I think that car-free or car-lite is one of the best ways to enjoy the city. So much of our city is held back by needing to have parking lots, we have a huge amount of untapped potential in our parking system and charging dynamic parking prices would be a great way to generate revenue and encourage people to drive less. We can also tie car registration to size or weight of vehicles, requiring vehicles that weigh more to pay more for road use.  I don’t think that government and private provision of housing are in conflict with one another. I know that frequently there is debate about if markets can provide enough housing at a low enough price point to house everyone, but I think that they can complement one another. Private housing induces affordability cascades that provide better units for lower rents in a neighborhood, not to mention the market has the capital DC does not to build enough housing to bring down rents. If Jubilee’s construction costs are standard, it would be almost $1 million per apartment built by the District. In 2025 there were almost 2,000 housing starts, a 15 year low,  which would mean DC needs to spend $2 billion a year, or one-sixth of its entire annual capital budget, just to match private housing starts in today’s post-DOGE, high interest-rate DC economy.  The District can provide counter-cyclical development during economic downturns that insure our housing is not at the whims of macroeconomic conditions. DHCD could also provide new-housing in low-investment areas that have difficulty attracting buyers. I do think that any District-owned housing should be revenue neutral or even positive. We have seen frequently with DHCD and DOB where buildings are allowed to fall into disrepair because they do not have the money to stay in good condition or because the political will to keep them up has dissipated. Allowing District-housing to be at the mercy of yearly budget debates, tax receipts, and voting cycles makes them vulnerable, they will need to be able to stand up on their own.

column12: Affordable housing is housing where some form of subsidy, income restriction, or rent regulation keeps the cost below 30% of the household's income. Market-rate housing has no such support. However, it's important to provide a variety of housing forms and types (multi-family buildings, duplexes, triplexes, single-family homes, and so on) in DC, particularly in neighborhoods that have good access to transit. For example, in my SMD, a two-bedroom unit in a co-op may be “affordable” relative to the single-family homes that are on the market. A variety of housing types within a neighborhood have many benefits; they not only allow a greater diversity of residents, but they enable people to stay in a neighborhood they like as their needs change. A young couple can move to a larger home and start a family, an older empty-nest household can downsize to an apartment or a condo, and so on.  The comprehensive plan and zoning code should be updated to allow as many housing and building types as possible. What is built will depend on the market.  More market-rate supply eases the upward pressure on rents/costs across the board. That means fewer households need assistance in the first place, and the subsidy dollars DC does spend reach further.

column38: Two things that don’t come through in the checkboxes. On Question 21: I am not hostile to historic preservation. That is the argument I make to my neighbors, and I think it is a better one than asking them to accept a tradeoff.

column12: Affordable housing, to me, is housing that's well-maintained and monitored to actually meet the needs of the people living in it, where the government or another entity steps in, whether through subsidy, income restrictions, or rent control, so that residents aren't stretched past what they can reasonably afford. Market-rate housing is left to private developers and the open market, without those same built-in protections for residents.  That said, I don't think government intervention has to be exclusive to what we label "affordable housing." I'd support the government stepping into market-rate pricing too, but only if it's structured so the savings actually reach the resident directly, not absorbed by a developer or landlord along the way. The distinction isn't that one type of housing is good and the other isn't. It's that any intervention needs guardrails ensuring the benefit lands with the person actually living there.

column35: The biggest issue in my SMD is one I think drives a lot of our other problems: vacant buildings and empty lots that have sat unused for years. This includes two large former residential complexes near Rhode Island Ave, along with smaller vacant lots scattered throughout the neighborhood and into neighboring SMDs.    These aren't just missed opportunities for housing. Empty buildings and lots become magnets for trash, unsafe conditions, and neglect, and of course, rats. Anyone who's lived here for a while knows exactly what these vacant spaces attract, and it's a problem that keeps coming up because the buildings just keep sitting there. That takes a toll on how safe people feel on their own block, and it wears down the pride people have in their neighborhood. The real problem is simple: we have buildings sitting empty instead of being put to use.  I know an ANC commissioner can't rezone a property or force an owner to build. What I can realistically do is use the position to keep pressure on. That means working directly with property owners, the zoning commission, and DC agencies to push these sites toward actual redevelopment under the mayor's new housing initiative, showing up consistently at the meetings where these decisions get made, and making sure my neighbors' voices are part of that conversation. It won't fix everything overnight, but a commissioner who won't let these lots be forgotten is a start.
column36: Two thousand constituents is a real number, but it isn't an excuse to govern by guesswork. My approach starts with treating outreach as the job, not an afterthought to it.  This is a neighborhood position, and I don't think it should be run like a political campaign built around my own personal platform. The decisions that come before an ANC, alley closures, zoning cases, liquor licenses, development proposals, affect real people on real blocks, and I believe those people should have a direct hand in shaping the outcome, not just a commissioner assuming they know best.  So my plan is simple and direct. I intend to go to every household in my SMD, in person, and give people a real chance to talk to me or leave their concerns behind, whether that's a conversation on their porch or a QR code they can use on their own time to reach me directly. I won't hear from all 2,000 people, and I won't pretend that whoever I do hear from speaks for everyone. But that outreach becomes the foundation I build from. It tells me what people are actually worried about, not what I assume they're worried about.  Beyond that first round of outreach, my job doesn't stop at listening once. I plan to actively work to get more people engaged with our meetings themselves, whether that means letting neighbors know when something on the agenda will actually affect them, or simply making meetings feel worth showing up to. A commissioner can't represent people who don't know a decision is being made. Part of representing this community well is making sure more of it knows what's happening and has a chance to weigh in before decisions get made, not after.  I won't have perfect information from every constituent. No commissioner does. But I'd rather build my decisions on direct, ongoing conversations with my neighbors than on my own convictions about what's best for a community I was elected to serve, not lead from the front of.
column37: I think I'm the right person for this because I'm not running on my own agenda, I'm running to actually listen and act on what my neighbors need. This is a neighborhood position, and I believe the decisions that come out of it should be shaped by the neighborhood, not by whatever platform I walked in with.  I'm personally affected by the same things most of my neighbors are: the cost of living in this city, the feeling that homeownership here is out of reach, and yes, sometimes that uneasy feeling walking home alone at night past a block that's been dark and empty for years. I'm not approaching these issues from a distance. I live them too.  What I bring to this role is a real plan to hear from people, not just the ones who already show up to meetings, but as many of my 2,000 neighbors as I can reach, and to use that input as the actual foundation for what I push for. I want to help build a neighborhood that feels safer to walk through, that people are proud to call home, and that actually has room for the people who want to live here.  I'm not looking to lead from the front. I'm looking to represent this community as it actually is, and fight for what it actually needs.
column38: Reliable, frequent, and affordable public transportation is one of the most impactful investments any city can make in its residents, and I will always push for greater access to it.  I'm also personally affected by the cost of living crushing this city, where rent and property costs are at the center of the problem. Right now, multiple empty lots sit unused throughout our SMD while people struggle to find housing they can afford. That land should be put to work now, and I'll push our zoning commission and ANC to make that happen.  But affordability can't just mean lower rent. I want to see real support for first-time homeowners, not investors buying a third property to rent out, but families and individuals trying to put down roots in DC, where homeownership currently feels like a joke to most residents. I'd advocate for subsidies and programs targeted specifically at first-time buyers who will actually live in and be part of this city.  I believe this matters beyond individual finances. When people have a real stake in their community, not just a lease renewal, they invest in it. They show up to ANC meetings, know their neighbors, and fight for their block, rather than treating DC as a transient stop or a place they resent for draining their paycheck. Homeownership access isn't just an economic issue for me. It's how we build a city people actually feel is theirs.

I want the One Big Idea to serve residents at 30% AMI, costing no more than 30% of their income for rent and utilities. column38: As I end my first ANC term, I would like to post an update on the situation that gave me the call to enter public service in 2024. In 2021, DC bought the property at 1339 Green Court, NW for use by the Department of Human Services (DHS) as a 150-bed, low-barrier, men's shelter. The site itself seemed to me to be wildly unsuitable for the purpose, and I persistently asked functional questions framed by the future safety of 150 of our most vulnerable neighbors:  1) contamination of the structure by 70 years as an industrial building;  2) alley-landlocked site with no sidewalks or pedestrian access;  3) limited access to firetrucks and emergency equipment;  4) alley lot zoning restrictions requiring challengeable variances; and 5) construction challenges with no space for a crane or construction material.  In early 2025,  my persistence led DHS to task the Department of General Services (DGS) to conduct a feasibility study of the property for use as a men's shelter. No funding has been allocated for a DGS study in the FY2025, FY2026, or FY2027 Budgets, effectively shelving the project indefinitely. In May 2026, DGS confirmed that 1339 Green Court has been removed from the DHS inventory and returned to DGS.  During the entire process, I pledged to find other sites in my own SMD 2C02 for use to address the needs of our unhoused neighbors. I am thrilled that Metropolitan AME Church, on the exterior surface of their historic church, is undertaking to build 27 units of Permanent Supportive Housing for Black veterans, and I have enthusiastically supported the initial stages of zoning variances which have been approved.

column12: As an ANC for over 10 years, I've witnessed Black and brown neighbors being systematically displaced by rising costs and weakened protections, and how much harder it is for seniors to age in place. But the need for affordable housing impacts everyone, across income levels, ages, and ethnicities.  To me, affordable housing means income-restricted, subsidized homes where families pay no more than 30% of their income and can live with dignity alongside market-rate residents and not warehoused in concentrated sites. Market-rate housing is unsubsidized and priced by the private market, with no income-eligibility requirements. The distinction matters most in how we deploy it.  At Bruce Monroe and Park Morton, we fought for a deliberate mix: replacement units for displaced Park Morton families, additional deeply affordable units, and market-rate housing alongside them. Mixed-income development helps keep a corridor economically diverse rather than gentrifying wholesale.  Affordable housing shouldn't mean "cheap." It should mean high-quality, dignified housing reachable for teachers, service workers, seniors, and long-term residents whose incomes haven't kept pace with rising costs. Market-rate development also plays a role, generating the density and revenue that can make projects like Bruce Monroe financially possible. ANCs play a critical role, and I look forward to continuing this work for Park Morton, Bruce Monroe, and beyond.

column12: While both market-rate and affordable housing are vital to a complete neighborhood ecosystem, they serve distinct functions driven by entirely different mechanisms.  Market-rate housing relies on private development and supply-demand cycles to house people at prevailing costs. It is essential because failing to build enough market-rate units only intensifies competition, bidding up prices on older housing stock and squeezing out middle-income households.  Affordable housing is deliberately structured through tools like Inclusionary Zoning, subsidies, or public intervention to decouple housing costs from speculative market pressures. It ensures that public servants, service workers, seniors, and healthcare professionals are not priced out of the communities they serve.  Ultimately, market-rate housing drives overall production and supply absorption, while affordable housing is an active equity tool that prevents displacement and keeps our neighborhoods economically diverse.

column12: Affordable housing carries an income restriction — a covenant, subsidy, or inclusionary set-aside tying rent to a share of area median income. Market-rate housing carries no such restriction. It’s not a difference in quality or in who deserves to live there, and "market-rate" does not inherently mean “expensive.” But market-rate rents are expensive here in DC, and that is a consequence of a choice we've made. When a region adds jobs and households faster than it adds homes, the existing stock gets auctioned off to whoever can bid highest. Scarcity doesn't ration housing by need; it rations by income. The result is that older buildings, which used to house teachers, service workers, and young families without any subsidy at all, get renovated and repriced — and the households they used to serve are pushed out or pushed further away. So the two categories are linked. Restricting supply doesn't preserve affordability; it destroys the unsubsidized affordability we already have and dumps the entire burden onto subsidy programs that can never be funded at the scale required. Every unit we don't build becomes a household competing for one that already exists. Dedicated affordable housing is essential — it's the only tool that reaches the lowest incomes, and I support expanding it. But it can't do the job alone. If we want market-rate housing to be affordable to anyone but the wealthiest, we have to build enough of it.

column12: I believe these characteristics can each be present in affordable housing, but none is a strict requirement on its own. Government can build affordable housing directly, but private developers play an equally important role here in the District through Inclusionary Zoning (IZ) requirements. Supporting both public and private approaches lets us expand the affordable housing supply faster to meet growing demand.  Market-rate and affordable housing are often framed as opposites, but I don't think that holds up cleanly. "Expensive" is relative to income, so market-rate housing isn't inherently unaffordable in every case. I also don't think market-rate status alone is a good reason to exempt a unit from rent control — being market-rate shouldn't, by itself, place a unit outside those protections. I support strengthening the District's rent control laws.

column14: To me, family-sized housing means units with enough bedrooms to comfortably accommodate multiple generations or multiple children, generally three or more, but that doesn't require large square footage. My SMD is full of semi-detached rowhomes that are modest in size but still offer two or three bedrooms, a meaningful step up from the studios and one-bedrooms that dominate so much of the District's newer housing stock. Family-sized housing doesn't mean sprawling floor plans; it can mean the right bedroom configuration in a compact footprint.  The District's housing stock is historically skewed toward studios and one-bedrooms, which pushes families with children toward the suburbs and erodes the intergenerational fabric of neighborhoods like the ones I represent in Ward 7. Family-sized housing also isn't only about the unit itself, it means proximity to what families need day to day: schools, parks, grocery stores, and reliable transit. I'd also note that "family" shouldn't be narrowly defined as parents with biological children. Grandparents raising grandchildren, multigenerational households, and blended families all need housing that fits their structure, and our affordable housing requirements should reflect that reality rather than a nuclear-family default. I support requiring a meaningful share of new affordable and mixed-income developments to include family-sized units, rather than letting developers concentrate compliance in studios and one-bedrooms.

column26: I believe there's significant opportunity for housing growth in ANC 7B toward meeting the presumptive mayor's goal, including in 7B03. I strongly believe we need to increase density along the Pennsylvania Ave SE corridor, serving two purposes: meeting growing demand for housing and delivering the economic development the Small Area Plan (SAP) has been working toward for over half a decade. While testifying at the BZA in favor of a zoning variance for a project on Pennsylvania Ave that added units to an existing building, I stated that I support the variance and that, more broadly, nothing on Pennsylvania Ave should be zoned R-1. As part of the SAP covering Pennsylvania Ave, a special zone was created between Fairlawn Ave and 27th St to make the corridor more attractive to developers building mixed-use spaces. In 2022, a developer purchased the old Alexander Pope Funeral Home at 2617 Pennsylvania Ave SE with plans to build a 4-story residential building. The developer has since walked away after demolishing the old building, and the lot now sits overgrown, attracting rodents and trash in our community. This is a prime location to add density in 7B03. I'd love to see ground-level retail with housing above; the lot is already inside the newly created NMU-5A/PAE zone and is shovel-ready. A 2nd strong site, elsewhere in 7B, is the parking lot behind Penn Branch Shopping Center. A proposal first floated in 2022 would have added 6,850 sq ft of ground-level retail with 175-185 single and family-sized rental units above, but it hasn't moved since. Housing and retail along this corridor go hand in hand: if we want the economic development the SAP envisions, we need the population to support it, and housing above retail builds in a customer base from day one. I'd support reviving this project. A 3rd opportunity is addressing the number of gas stations along Pennsylvania Ave. Along the 1.3-mile stretch between Fairlawn and Alabama Aves, there are six gas stations, four clustered in just the two blocks between Fairlawn and Minnesota Aves. That's too many for this stretch of road, and it's not the best use of prime real estate along the corridor. I would support the District making it easier to convert some of these sites to mixed-use buildings, while being mindful that in some cases, these stations are also a nearby source of basic groceries or snacks in areas that are food deserts, so any conversion should account for that gap rather than simply ignoring this reality. If we could reclaim even half of these sites, it would let us build dozens of new retail spaces and hundreds of new housing units. Between the Alexander Pope site, the Penn Branch redevelopment, and reclaiming even a portion of these underused gas station lots, ANC 7B has a clear and achievable path to not just meet, but exceed, the numbers needed to help the incoming mayor meet this goal while also delivering the retail and economic development our community has been waiting on for years.

column34: In 2024, I committed to using Capital Bikeshare more often for ANC meetings, site visits, and nearby errands. I've followed through on the errands piece — I now default to Bikeshare or bus over driving for nearly everything in the District, since I've never found the car easier than a bikeshare or a bus once you factor in city parking. ANC meetings and site visits have been slower to fully shift, though I've been biking to more of them over the past several months. This year, I'm committing to biking to ANC 7B meetings and related site visits as my default, rather than defaulting to the car as I sometimes still do out of habit or timing. Between this and my existing transit habits — I rely on WMATA for essentially all work travel, including Capitol Hill visits — the car has become the exception rather than the default for how I get around the District.
column35: The number of vacant and blighted properties in 7B03 that sit neglected for years, in some cases decades, with nothing done about them. Some have roofs actively collapsing. Because many are rowhomes or semi-detached properties physically attached to other, occupied homes, their decay actively threatens the structural integrity of the neighboring homes they're attached to. This isn't just an eyesore; it's a safety hazard, it depresses surrounding property values, and it represents housing stock that should be part of the solution to our affordability crisis instead of sitting empty and rotting. I don't think the District can credibly talk about a 72,000-unit housing goal while doing so little to activate the vacant properties we already have. This sits alongside two other issues I hear about constantly: residual problems from the Better Bus rollout — stops without shelters, routes that don't serve our community's actual needs, and frequencies that leave residents underserved — and moments where our community has felt outright forgotten by the District, like this year when several 7B03 streets went unplowed for several days after an ice storm until I personally intervened. No resident should feel forgotten by their own government.  Continue pushing DCRA and the Department of Buildings to aggressively enforce vacant and blighted property fines, and advocate for the District to move toward demolishing the most dangerous derelict structures and billing the owners directly, rather than letting properties sit indefinitely while fines go unpaid. As a Commissioner, I don't have direct enforcement authority, but I can and will keep filing 311 reports, testifying at relevant hearings, and putting public pressure on DCRA through ANC resolutions to escalate enforcement on the worst offenders in 7B03. On Better Bus and snow removal, I'll continue what I've already been doing: submitting formal resolutions like 7B-24-03 to WMATA with specific route and shelter requests, and directly advocating with DDOT and DPW when our streets are neglected, as I did this year to get 7B03 streets plowed. Commissioners don't control these agencies, but sustained, specific, public pressure gets results, and I intend to keep applying it.
column36: I approach decision-making as a mix of active outreach, transparency, and honesty about uncertainty rather than assuming silence means consent or that the loudest voices in the room represent the whole SMD. First, I try to widen who I actually hear from, rather than relying only on those who show up to ANC meetings, which tend to skew toward retirees, homeowners, and people with fewer scheduling constraints. That means using tools like community surveys, as I did with the Pennsylvania Avenue/Minnesota Avenue intersection redesign, canvassing directly on specific issues, and using social media and listservs to reach residents who will never attend a meeting but will respond to a direct, low-effort ask. Second, when I do hear from constituents, I try to distinguish between a genuine cross-section of opinion and an organized or vocal minority. A dozen passionate emails on one side of an issue isn't the same as a representative sample, and I try to be honest with myself and with residents about which one I'm looking at before I treat it as a mandate. Third, on issues where I can't get meaningful direct input, because perhaps they're too technical, too fast-moving, or too under-the-radar for most residents to weigh in, I rely on established public policy principles, and my own professional background in advocacy and compliance work to make a judgment call, and I try to explain that reasoning publicly rather than hiding behind "constituent feedback" I don't actually have. Finally, I believe part of the job is proactively surfacing issues before they become emergencies, rather than only reacting to what constituents happen to bring to me. The snow removal and vacant property issues in 7B03 are good examples: most residents don't think to email their Commissioner about unplowed streets or a rotting rowhouse next door, but part of representing them well is noticing these problems myself, investigating, and acting without waiting for a critical mass of complaints. Ultimately, I try to make decisions I can defend publicly and explain clearly, not just decisions that reflect whoever emailed me last, because being a good representative means using your judgment responsibly when you don't and can't have a full picture of every constituent's view.
column37: I've been the Commissioner for 7B03 since 2021, and active in this community even longer, involved with the Randle Highlands Citizens Civic Association since 2015. I've spent this term proving I show up for this community, not just at ANC meetings, but in the details that make a real difference. When DDOT proposed expanding the Pennsylvania/Minnesota Avenues intersection from 8 to 10 lanes, I didn't just object, I helped pass multiple unanimous ANC resolutions, ran a community survey, hosted a public meeting, wrote publicly about it, and pushed the issue directly to DDOT's Director. We didn't win that fight, but I don't shy away from taking on the District's biggest agencies even when the odds are long. When DDOT proposed closing access to 25th Street from Pennsylvania Ave as part of that same project, I pushed back and won, keeping that access open. Professionally, I bring my government relations and advocacy background to the table locally: I know how to navigate bureaucracy, build coalitions, and apply sustained pressure on agencies that would rather residents stay quiet. I've put those same skills to use reading the fine print on zoning cases, BZA filings, and District regulations, and testifying on cases directly affecting our SMD. I'm not new to this work, and I'm not doing it for a resume line. I've spent a decade building relationships and understanding of this community, and I'm asking for the chance to keep putting that experience to work for Randle Highlands.
column38: A few additional notes to round out my answers above. On Q10, I checked all four combinations because I consider public ownership of the land and the housing itself to be the defining feature of social housing, not who performs construction or day-to-day management. As long as the District retains ownership and control of the underlying asset, it can guarantee the unit stays permanently off the speculative market and set the terms such as rent levels, tenant protections, and eligibility regardless of who was contracted to build or manage it. This mirrors systems like Vienna's Gemeindebau and Singapore's HDB, which routinely use private contractors while remaining unambiguously public housing. Contracting out can be a practical necessity given the District's limited in-house capacity, and I don't think that should disqualify a unit from being considered social housing as long as public ownership remains the anchor, though I'd support strong contractual and oversight requirements on any private management company to ensure accountability isn't lost in the handoff.  I answered "enough" on Q12 regarding historic districts, but I want to be clear about what that reflects. ANC 7B doesn't currently have any historic districts, so "enough" is accurate to my SMD today, but it also reflects my broader view. I don't support expanding historic district designations. There's a meaningful difference between a building or landmark having historic significance worth preserving, and designating entire zones or neighborhoods as historic, which can be used to broadly restrict housing development and density. I'd rather see preservation tools used narrowly, for individual structures that genuinely warrant it, than applied at the neighborhood scale. My answer to Q15 also doesn't fully capture my view on car ownership. The realistic number of vehicles a family needs varies depending on where in the District they live and what transit is available; a family in 7B03 is in a different position than one steps from a Metro station. Rather than assume a single "right" number citywide, I'd rather see the District focus on making zero or one vehicle a realistic choice everywhere, through better bus frequency, protected bike infrastructure, and safer pedestrian access. On Q27 and Q28, I selected the options indicating I would introduce a resolution in support of dedicated bus lanes and protected bike lanes, and want to be clear that isn't hypothetical, I've already written and passed resolutions on these issues. Looking ahead, two priorities for the next two years: working with DDOT and NPS to finally implement resolution 7B-23-05, which calls for pedestrian and cyclist improvements on 27th Street between Naylor Road and Texas Avenue and has passed but seen no real movement; and pushing for real action on the vacant and blighted houses in 7B03 I've raised repeatedly. I'm proud of the work I've done on these issues, and I look forward to continuing it if reelected.

column12: I believe affordable housing and market-rate housing serve different but equally important purposes in a healthy community.  I know what it's like to reside in unhealthy conditions, work and save to change that.  Affordable housing is intended to ensure that lower- and moderate-income individuals and families are not priced out of the neighborhoods where they live and work. Its cost is generally tied to household income or established affordability standards rather than simply what the private market will bear.  Market-rate housing, by contrast, is generally priced according to supply, demand, location, and overall market conditions without an affordability requirement or subsidy.  I do not believe these two forms of housing should be viewed as being in competition with one another. Washington needs housing at different income levels. Responsible growth should provide opportunities for new residents while protecting longtime residents from displacement and respecting the character of established neighborhoods.  My goal is a diverse, mixed-income community where working families, seniors, young professionals, and people at different income levels have an opportunity to call the neighborhood home.

column14: To me, family-sized housing means housing that gives families enough space, stability, and affordability to put down roots and remain part of their community as their needs change.  It generally means homes with two, three, or more bedrooms, but bedroom count alone does not make housing family-friendly. Families also need adequate living and storage space, safe buildings, and reasonable access to transportation, schools, childcare, parks, recreation, groceries, and other everyday necessities.  In a growing neighborhood like Ivy City, I believe new residential development should include a meaningful number of units designed for families. If most new housing consists only of studios and one-bedroom apartments, it becomes difficult for households to remain in the neighborhood as their families grow.  Family-sized housing should also exist at different price points, including affordable and market-rate options. A strong neighborhood should provide opportunities for families of different incomes and at different stages of life.  Ultimately, family-sized housing means creating homes where people can establish roots, raise children, build relationships with their neighbors, and become long-term members of the community.

column23: I support building more housing in the District, including apartments, but I do not believe that every type of housing is appropriate on every block of every neighborhood.  Washington is a city of very different neighborhoods, each with its own character, infrastructure, transportation access, street configuration, historic resources, and existing housing patterns. A zoning policy that automatically allows six-unit apartment buildings everywhere does not adequately recognize those differences.  I support greater density and multifamily housing in appropriate locations, particularly along major corridors, near public transportation, and in areas where infrastructure can accommodate additional residents. I also support creating more affordable and family-sized housing.  At the same time, residents should have a meaningful voice when significant zoning changes are proposed for established residential neighborhoods. New development should consider parking, traffic, pedestrian safety, schools, utilities, public transportation, and the existing character of the surrounding community.  We can increase Washington's housing supply without adopting a one-size-fits-all approach. I favor thoughtful growth that creates more homes while respecting the characteristics and needs of individual neighborhoods.

column26: I believe Ivy City can accommodate additional housing, but where and how it is built matters.  Rather than dramatically increasing density on established residential blocks, I would prioritize underutilized commercial and industrial properties, vacant or redevelopment-ready parcels, and locations along major transportation corridors where additional density can be accommodated responsibly.  Ivy City has historically contained a mixture of residential, commercial and industrial uses. As some properties transition away from older industrial uses, we have an opportunity to consider mixed-use redevelopment that can provide new housing while also bringing neighborhood-serving retail, services and public improvements.  Any significant residential development should take infrastructure into consideration, including public transportation, parking, traffic, pedestrian safety, utilities, schools and other services. I would also want new development to include a meaningful mix of housing, including affordable and family-sized units, rather than concentrating exclusively on studios and small apartments.  I do not believe meeting a citywide housing target should mean simply assigning an arbitrary number of units to every neighborhood regardless of local conditions. However, I believe Ivy City can contribute to Washington's housing needs through thoughtful development in appropriate locations.  My goal would be to add housing while preserving Ivy City's identity, protecting existing residents and businesses, and ensuring that new development contributes positively to the community.

column35: Public safety and quality of life are the biggest issues facing Ivy City. We need effective law enforcement, but enforcement alone will not solve every problem. We also need greater access to mental-health and substance-use professionals, stronger educational opportunities, and better coordination among District agencies.  One example is the alley adjacent to the shelter in Ivy City. Poor management of this area has contributed to persistent drug activity, violence, public health and sanitation concerns, and other dangerous behavior that affects shelter residents, neighborhood residents, employees, and businesses. We must address these conditions while treating people experiencing homelessness, addiction, or mental-health crises with dignity and connecting them with appropriate services.  Parking and transportation decisions are also significant quality-of-life concerns for residents and businesses. At the same time, I want Ivy City to have more positive community activities, including arts, music, cultural events, youth programs, and neighborhood festivals.  I believe public safety means creating a neighborhood that is safe, clean, welcoming, and active for everyone.  If elected, I would use the ANC's influence and my relationships with District agencies to aggressively advocate for solutions while recognizing that an ANC commissioner cannot directly command MPD or other agencies.  I would document recurring problems, bring them formally before the ANC, request agency action and written follow-up, introduce or support ANC resolutions when appropriate, and maintain regular communication with MPD, DDOT, DPW, DBH, DHS and other agencies responsible for the issues affecting Ivy City.  For the shelter and surrounding area, I would push for coordinated action involving law enforcement, homeless-services providers, mental-health and substance-use professionals, sanitation services, shelter management, residents, and businesses. My goal would be both accountability and getting people who need help connected with appropriate services.  I would also advocate for practical solutions to parking and pedestrian-safety problems and work to bring more arts, educational programs, community events, and family-friendly activities to Ivy City.  Most importantly, I would follow up. Referring a constituent to an agency is not enough. I would track problems, communicate progress publicly, and continue pressing for action until residents receive an answer.
column36: An ANC commissioner represents the entire community, not simply the residents who attend meetings or speak the loudest. If elected, I will make a deliberate effort to hear from people throughout my district before making important decisions.  I believe representation requires going to the community rather than expecting the community to always come to you. I will regularly walk the neighborhood, speak directly with residents and local businesses, attend community events, and use meetings, social media, email, surveys, and direct outreach to seek input. I will make a particular effort to reach people who may never attend an ANC meeting.  When an important issue arises, I will seek information from multiple sources. I will listen to those who support a proposal and those who oppose it, review the facts, consult District agencies and subject-matter experts when appropriate, and consider both the immediate and long-term consequences for Ivy City.  I will not assume that the loudest voices necessarily represent the majority. At the same time, leadership sometimes requires making a difficult decision after listening to everyone and carefully examining the facts.  Transparency will be fundamental to how I serve. Residents should know what issues are before the ANC, what position I take, why I take it, and what actions I am pursuing on their behalf.  My commitment is simple: **Your voice will always be heard.** That does not mean everyone will always agree with every decision I make. It means every constituent will be treated with respect, given an opportunity to be heard, and represented fairly—whether they voted for me or not.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as ANC Commissioner because Ivy City is not simply where I am running for office—it is my home and a community I have been deeply involved with for years.  I've lived in Ivy City since 2016 and worked in the neighborhood for more than a decade. As a Director of Operations, I've experienced solving problems, managing people and budgets, working with government agencies, and bringing people with different interests together.  My commitment to public safety is demonstrated through years of cooperation with Ward 5 MPD, including providing video analysis and digital evidence that has assisted investigations. In 2025, MPD recognized me as a Ward 5 Outstanding Citizen for those efforts.  My connection to Ward 5 also goes back generations. My ancestors settled here, my father grew up in Ward 5, and members of my family are buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Ivy City. Serving this community is personal to me.  Most importantly, I am accessible. I walk these streets, speak with residents and businesses, see our challenges firsthand, and believe constituent concerns deserve follow-through, not just promises.  I will bring experience, energy, transparency, accountability, and a unique, left-handed, right brain burst of creativity bundled in an ANC. Whether someone agrees with me or not, **their voice will always be heard.**
column38: My answers reflect a belief that Washington can grow without losing sight of the people and neighborhoods that make the city successful. I support creating more housing, including affordable and family-sized housing, and I welcome responsible development. At the same time, I do not believe every housing or land-use policy should be applied identically to every neighborhood.  Ivy City has a unique mixture of residential, commercial and industrial uses. New development can bring housing, jobs, neighborhood-serving businesses and investment, but residents and existing businesses should have a meaningful voice in how that growth occurs. I support greater density where appropriate while also respecting neighborhood character, infrastructure limitations and historic resources.  My transportation positions follow a similar principle of balance. I strongly support reliable public transportation, safer streets, walking and bicycle infrastructure. However, I do not believe improving one form of transportation should automatically require making another form unnecessarily difficult. Residents, seniors, families, employees and businesses have different transportation needs. In Ivy City, parking is already a significant concern, and eliminating additional parking without considering the consequences can create new problems rather than solve existing ones.  I believe government should provide people with better transportation choices rather than dictate one choice for everyone.  As an ANC Commissioner, I would approach housing, transportation and land-use decisions individually, listen to residents and businesses, examine the facts, and work toward practical compromises. I am pro-growth, but I believe growth should be responsible, inclusive and beneficial to the community that is being asked to accommodate it.  My goal is an Ivy City that welcomes new neighbors and investment while remaining a place where existing residents, families and businesses can continue to thrive.

column12: My point of view is that market-rate housing is priced at what the market will bear. It is an important component in increasing the city’s tax base and in creating an affordable city. For example, when Austin added roughly 120,000 homes over about ten years, the rents in Class C buildings fell 11.4% and Class A rents fell 2.6%. In contrast, affordable housing is priced below that through subsidy, regulation, or building age. There are a variety of policy handles to create affordability and they need to be used correctly. Inclusionary zoning can reach roughly 50–80% of AMI before new housing development does not pencil out and nothing gets built. Deeply affordable units – which are also needed – require direct public investment rather than a requirement added onto private development. In my opinion, this is why the Office of Planning correctly proposed exempting projects with a one-third deep-affordability set-aside from design review in ZC 25-13.

column35: The biggest issue is housing cost, and I think it's fundamentally a supply problem. Ward 3 has not built its share of housing over the last decade and the result is priced into every house and apartment.  A commissioner's formal authority is advisory, but it’s real and can be effective. In ZC 25-13, I worked with colleagues to shape the ANC's resolution and filed my own comment with the Zoning Commission arguing that design-review criteria should be objective and measurable, so large corridor projects aren't tied up for years by standards no architect can design to. I'd apply the same approach to gentle density: bring my colleagues along where I can, and make the record myself where I can't.
column36: I hear from constituents through ANC meetings, neighborhood events, and organizations like the Cleveland Park Community Association. I have found being active and introducing resolutions helps get people involved and wanting to share their opinions.  But I try to weigh this input carefully. The people who come to a Tuesday evening ANC meeting are not a random sample of my 2,000 constituents. They skew toward homeowners, longer-tenured residents, and people with the time and flexibility to attend. Renters, younger residents, people working evening shifts, and people with small children are often underrepresented but they also have a lot at stake. Also not present are the future residents who could live here if there was more housing. So I treat what I hear as important evidence, not as a vote count. Where the input I receive conflicts with what I think serves the ANC and the district as a whole, I say so and explain why. On ZC 25-13, several of the loudest voices wanted more discretionary design review. I concluded that vague, unmeasurable review criteria would delay or block housing development on Wisconsin Avenue and raise costs for people who aren't at our meetings — including people who don't live here yet because they can't afford to – and the comments I filed individually said that. I also try to weigh input I can check against evidence — Office of Planning capacity analysis, zoning case records, election data — rather than relying only on impressions from the people who reach me.
column37: I served a previous term as commissioner so I think there is a track record I can point to of doing the homework, making arguments on the merits, listening to my colleagues respectfully and bringing them along where possible, being willing to say what I think, and introducing substantive resolutions. I'd rather be persuasive than loud. For example, on ZC 25-13, I read the Office of Planning's supplemental report closely enough to notice that its exemption for deeply affordable projects conceded the argument about discretionary review's cost — and I used that to make the case to my colleagues. I proposed amendments to our resolution rather than introducing a competing one, worked through several drafts with the commissioner who authored it, and we ended up passing something 5-0 that asked the Zoning Commission for clear standards and a defined timetable. Where the ANC chose not to take a substantive position, I filed my own comment so the argument was in the record. I think this is what being an effect ANC Commissioner requires.
column38: I would like to go into more detail on a couple of questions. Re the National Week Without Driving. I declined not because I disagree with the goal but because I try not to commit to things I'm not confident I'll do. We have two young children and most weeks a car trip isn't optional. What I will commit to is the policy work, which I think matters more: I'd introduce resolutions supporting dedicated bus lanes, protected bike lanes, and road pricing, and shifting more of my own grocery trips to foot. Re the affordable housing question. I checked rent control because it does produce below market rents, but I'd distinguish it from the other mechanisms listed because it isn’t be targeted by need. It may also not be that effective at producing below market rents: the Office of Revenue Analysis found rent control only delivers about a 4.6% discount against comparable Class B market-rate stock. I'd rather deliver deep affordability through direct public investment in order to reach the households that need it.

column12: In theory, housing could be both market-rate and affordable. But when housing is market-rate, it’s functioning primarily as a commodity, which I consider unethical and unlikely to produce sufficient and timely affordability. Interventions like rent control, housing vouchers, or the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (TOPA) help blunt market-rate impacts, but are constantly eroded by market pressures and landlord lobbying. I believe long-lasting affordability and quality will only come from treating housing as a public good (like libraries or air quality) rather than as a commodity. That would mean publicly directed and/or financed construction, limiting the ability to use residences as investment vehicles, tenant control of property management, and more. In the meantime, I support building as much housing as possible under the Inclusionary Zoning (IZ) Affordable Housing Program, since that’s the best tool on the books that I know of. I’m eager to negotiate in Board of Zoning Adjustment (BZA) cases for voluntary inclusionary units and/or for additional units on new developments in order to trigger the IZ thresholds.

I think “family-sized housing” ought to include configurations that support those dynamics as well. And that goes beyond bedrooms; it can mean multiple kitchens, or common space shared among dormitory units, or accessory dwelling units. I also want us to think outside the lot; family housing includes good parks, schools, and other amenities nearby, because it truly does take a village and we should design our environments accordingly. So, overall, I think family-sized housing should mean housing that fits people’s varied needs, rather than housing that forces people to contort or compress their lives.

column35: My target issue is the stiflingly high rent, both commercial and residential, that keeps our storefronts empty and our residents over-burdened. I think this high rent will limit the possible businesses, especially small, new, and local businesses, at that location in a way that is detrimental to the neighborhood. column36: First, I want my constituents to know that outreach and communication is a top priority for me in the near future. column37: I don’t know if I’m the best person to be Commissioner. But last election, as in so many SMDs, I was the only one who volunteered. My reason for volunteering again is the same: I want to serve my neighborhood and my city. Over my first term, I’ve been energized by the chance to help folks. In an atomized and alienated society like ours, I see the hyperlocal structure of ANCs as a seed for community restoration. In my 11 years of political organizing, the most effective leaders bring a combination of bureaucratic skill and social cohesion. I’ve always had an analytical mind, which has served me well in my physics major, software engineering career, and (most importantly) board game night. I think it has aided me greatly in my research and application of ANC duties, zoning regulations, governmental structures, and policy matters. But I left software because I’m disgusted by the industry’s ethics. Flock cameras, generative AI, “educational” tech, pervasive social media, invasive advertising, and Palantir mercenaries are driving us into a societal pit of despair. With 4C back in financial compliance and with a firm sense of the ANC role, I want to move beyond the bureaucratic and into the community. I’ll draw upon the same skills I used as a leader of Sunrise Movement DC, where I applied consensus-based decision making, hosted social events, fostered relationships with other organizations, and met people with warmth and an open mind. Let’s build a community, not just houses.

column38: On Question #29 on congestion pricing, I'm more undecided with a tinge of cautious support, so I took the least committed "yes" answer on that one. I fully accept that congestion pricing has been great for New York City, and I agree with the theory behind congestion pricing. However, the 2021 DC study was outdated by the time Mayor Bowser released it 5 years later. I think a new study is warranted that can take into account post-COVID traffic and commuting patterns and also look to NYC's experience, and I'm not saying "a new study is needed" in a NIMBY-like way just to delay, delay, delay. Even if economically valid, I'm also very cautious about moving forward with congestion pricing due to Congressional interference. Politically, it would require buy-in from the Representatives and Senators of our neighbors in Virginia and Maryland. Many Congresspeople would love to use their unethical power to overturn our local laws too, so congestion pricing would have to be passed at a favorable time and implemented rapidly. Overall, I'm not as anti-car as many pro-housing urbanists are though. I'm a car owner. I love having my car. I'm not going to give it up. I travel to the outer suburbs a few times a month on average. What takes me an hour in my car would take 2 transfers and 2 hours by public transportation or $60 by rideshare each way. I think residents should be able to have cars if they want them. However, I think we should make DC a city where cars aren't as necessary so that most people can live comfortably without them. I support dedicated bus lanes and protected bike lanes even though I don't often ride the bus and don't own a bike. I don't think it's a contradiction to support bike-friendly and public transportation-friendly policies while also continuing to make owning and using a car an option that one can choose, even if it's a bit more of a hassle or having to pay a bit of a premium. Along those same lines, I'm in favor of robotaxis. There are certainly questions on how to best implement them, but I'd rather they be permitted sooner rather than later. On Question #5, I said my ANC has "enough homes". As elaborated in some of my other answers, ANC 1A is the densest in DC. If anybody wants to develop a property to make it denser, I'll of course be supportive, but DC's focus should be on making most other neighborhoods denser. Lastly, on Question #12 on historic districts, ANC 1A only slightly overlaps with the Meridian Hill Historic District. It affects only about 3.5 blocks in ANC 1A, some of which are owned by embassies, so it's not a significant issue in this ANC. I would probably be supportive of at least reducing the part labeled "historic" in ANC 1A though.

Our neighborhood is a hotspot for illegal dumping and neighbors often reach out to me about DPW missing their entire alley’s trash during collection days. When neighbors reach out to their city agencies, we deserve to be heard and responded to - just as much as every other ward in D.C.  Since I’ve been serving as my neighborhood’s Commissioner, I’ve made it my number one priority to build strong relationships with district agencies and Councilmember Felder’s Office to bring long-over due attention to Rosedale. I’ve organized multiple community cleanups alongside Councilmember Felder and DPW, I’ve worked with district agencies to lead a Public Safety Walk throughout our SMD, and I’ve helped advocate for new pilot programs, like the Roving Clean Team, which gives Rosedale dedicated attention from street sweepers. We’ve worked together to address multiple scofflaw vehicles, removing dangerous and abandoned vehicles from the streets. And we’ve worked with DOB to enforce that property owners do their part in securing abandoned properties that make it a safe haven for illegal activity.  As Commissioner, I will continue to bridge the gap between residents and their government, while consistently advocating for our neighborhood’s fair share of attention and resources from the District. column36: I’m not sure I accept the notion that our representative can’t connect with all residents in an SMD. I have yet to meet a neighbor who opposes those values, and I lead every discussion or position I have with that starting point. column37: Rosedale is my home. The people who share this home with me have become more than just neighbors, they have become my community - even like family to me. When I purchased my home in this neighborhood nearly 4 years ago, I quickly recognized the almost-intentional lack of dedicated resources, services, and care for our neighborhood from District agencies. When I’d pick up litter along my street, I’d hear long-time neighbors say “good luck, the city will never help us.” And often they were right, we were missing leadership to advocate for these issues on our behalf.  Since becoming Commissioner in January of 2026, our neighborhood has made so much progress in addressing chronic issues related to trash collection, alley conditions, traffic safety, abandoned vehicles and homes - all symptoms of an unhealthy neighborhood. We still have a lot of work to do, especially in the scope of public safety, but I believe the investments I’ve made with Councilmember Felder and agency leaders at DPW, DOB, and DGS are the unlock to finding real solutions that better the lives of every Rosedale resident in SMD 7D06.
column38: I think often our conversation on housing, transportation, and land use ignores incorporating the experiences and points of view of the residents who actually live in the SMD being discussed. A desirable community is one where people can comfortably live, feel safe in their homes, and afford to stay long-term to build stability for themselves.  On housing, I do believe we should build more if we want to be a neighborhood where people of all income levels, life stages, and family sizes can afford to live. It’s how we create healthy neighborhoods. That means it is critical to build both affordable and market-rate homes. At the same time, I don't think responsible growth means dismissing concerns of current residents and home-owners who have the best pulse check on their neighborhood. We shouldn’t ignore their concerns for the sake of anyone’s unchecked bias for development. Good planning should take seriously our neighbor’s questions about public safety, traffic, infrastructure, neighborhood character, tree canopies and green space, construction impacts, and the cumulative effect of development on a block or neighborhood. Residents should have a meaningful voice, and that process should be about improving proposals rather than simply deciding whether change happens at all. On transportation, I come at this from a somewhat different perspective because I don't own a car. I value having safe, convenient alternatives to driving, and I want to see continued investment in transit, sidewalks, crosswalks, and safer streets. But I don't think the people who drive should be treated as the problem. Many neighbors depend on cars for work, caregiving, disability, errands, or other parts of their lives. A good transportation policy should give people more choices without making everyday life harder for those who need or choose to drive. More broadly, I want to approach these issues with curiosity rather than a predetermined ideological answer. The best outcome won't always be the one that most neatly fits into a particular policy category. As an ANC commissioner, I want to understand the evidence, listen to residents with different experiences, and weigh neighborhood impacts alongside the larger need for safety and growth in our neighborhood. For me, a win is when a neighborhood can keep existing residents in place, change and grow in a well thought out and careful way, and can welcome new residents without making current residents feel like their concerns no longer matter. I think we can do both and I approach the ANC with that balance in mind.

column35: In my opinion, the biggest issue in our neighborhood is pedestrian safety. North Capitol Street is functionally a highway that cuts through the middle of a residential neighborhood. The road encourages dangerous, high-speed driving, and the sidewalks and pedestrian infrastructure are terrible. First Street NW is better, but by no means ideal—drivers routinely ignore stop signs, and there is minimal traffic calming infrastructure. The result is an environment that is hostile to pedestrians and the neighborhood, and that serves no one except for out-of-state drivers speeding through our community.  I have passed resolutions and advocated with the DC government for several changes, and will continue to do so if reelected. Those include permanent traffic calming infrastructure on First ST NW, including speed bumps, raised crosswalks, stop-sign cameras, and permanent sidewalk bump-outs; and a full overhaul of North Capitol St NW, including sidewalk expansions, protected bus lanes, increased mixed-use zoning, and (once federal funding is once again a realistic possibility) a deck-over or full “community boulevard” conversion.
column36: Resident input is invaluable for knowing where safety improvements are most needed, and I often seek (and will continue to seek) resident input to know where to target my advocacy for pedestrian safety improvements. But when it comes to issues like increasing density, expanding transit access, or permitting businesses to operate, I think Commissioners often hear from a very small group of residents who are opposed to improvements that would benefit the community as a whole. If I believe a zoning or transit change would benefit the community and I hear opposition from a small group of opponents, I will still support the change. However, if I were to hear widespread opposition from a very large cross-section of the community, then I would more seriously reconsider my support for the proposal.
column37: I am a passionate advocate for pedestrian safety, transit access, and economic opportunity. I also understand how deeply unaffordable our city has become—in my day job, I am a union lawyer, and I know that working people are being increasingly priced out of DC. As a lawyer, I fight to make sure they are paid fairly for their labor. And as a Commissioner, I fight (and will continue to fight) to make sure our city builds enough housing to ensure that working people are not forced to spend most of that fair pay just to afford a place to live.

I think well-implemented bike lanes not only add space for cyclists but also slow down traffic, making streets safer for everyone. I do also think, though, that it has to be done thoughtfully: in the right locations and in ways that don't cut off access for drivers, delivery vehicles, or residents who depend on cars. A key part of the job is hearing the most pressing concerns and using the authority of the office to elevate them — I'd like to start a monthly newsletter, and maybe even hold "office hours" at local businesses for residents who'd like to meet face-to-face. Commissioners don't control city agencies or set citywide policy, but we have real leverage through formal input and by virtue of just being a visible elected official. However, I do believe that where land is available, we should consider a mix of housing types that increases density while fitting the surrounding community. Looking at the ANC as a whole, I believe we do have the capacity for additional housing, particularly near Metro stations and along major transit corridors. Residents in Ward 7 are often told that we do not have enough population density or household income to support the grocery stores, restaurants, and retail that our communities need. At the same time, much of the new housing approved in Ward 7 is 100% affordable housing. While affordable housing is necessary, repeatedly concentrating deeply affordable housing in the same communities can reinforce economic segregation rather than create mixed-income neighborhoods. New housing in our ANC should include affordable, workforce, market-rate, family-sized, and homeownership opportunities. It should also be located near Metro and reliable public transportation, where residents have greater access to employment, services, and opportunities throughout the city. If we are going to significantly increase housing in Ward 7, we should use that growth to create stronger, mixed-income, transit-oriented communities that can also support the retail and amenities residents have long been asking for.

column34: One trip I would like to transition from driving to biking is my commute from Ward 7 to Howard University. My goal is to be able to make that trip safely and consistently by bike. However, Ward 7 still lacks sufficient protected bike infrastructure and safe, continuous connections to communities west of the Anacostia River. Much of the transportation infrastructure separating Ward 7 from the rest of the city reflects a history of inequitable investment and physical barriers between communities. If the District expects residents to reduce car trips, it must also address these disparities by creating protected bike lanes and safer connections across the river and into the city’s major employment centers. With better infrastructure, I would commit to biking to work regularly instead of driving. Reducing car dependency should be possible for residents in every ward, not just those who already live in communities with strong bicycle and transit infrastructure.
column35: The biggest issue in my neighborhood is the lack of grocery stores, healthy food options, and other basic retail. I believe this is directly connected to the continued concentration of poverty in Ward 7. Decisions by the Council and mayoral administrations have allowed a disproportionate amount of deeply affordable housing to be concentrated east of the river without enough mixed-income development, jobs, retail, and amenities to support these communities.  Affordable housing is necessary, but no community should be expected to carry a disproportionate share of the city’s poverty. Ward 7 needs a more balanced approach to development that creates economically diverse neighborhoods and supports the services residents have long been asking for.  Advocate for the kind of investment that allows residents to not just live in our community, but actually enjoy living here. That means better access to quality schools, jobs, recreation, healthy food, and places to shop and gather close to home. Residents should not have to leave Ward 7 for many of the basic things other parts of the city already have. I would also push for balanced development that brings a mix of affordable, market-rate, family-sized, and homeownership opportunities. As a commissioner, I know I cannot fix these issues alone, but I can use the position to keep pressure on city agencies, developers, and elected leaders, and make sure our community’s needs are consistently represented.
