column35: The biggest issue in my neighborhood is ensuring that every resident can safely and fully access the public resources our city provides. My SMD includes the Petworth and Upshur recreation centers, McFarland, Roosevelt, Dorothy Height, and Powell schools, the Petworth Library, and the Upshur Street commercial corridor. Because of this, the needs throughout my SMD are varied, but all tether to the fact that these spaces should be community anchors—safe, welcoming, well-maintained, and accessible to residents of every age, income, background, and ability. Access means more than having a facility nearby; it means that the space is functioning, residents know what is available, programs reflect community needs, and safety concerns do not prevent people from using it.  I would continue serving as a connector, advocate, and accountability partner between residents and District agencies. I would proactively seek input from people who may not regularly attend ANC meetings, identify barriers to accessing neighborhood facilities and services, and help residents navigate the agencies responsible for addressing them. I would use ANC resolutions, budget testimony, agency relationships, public meetings, and persistent follow-up to advocate for safe facilities, timely repairs, inclusive programming, accessible information, and responsible investment in our neighborhood. Because commissioners do not directly operate schools, libraries, recreation centers, or commercial corridors, I would be honest about the limits of the role while using its visibility and convening power to bring residents, agencies, schools, businesses, and community organizations together around practical solutions.
column36: I do not assume that the people who attend an ANC meeting or email me most frequently necessarily represent the full community. When an issue has broad implications, I try to create accessible ways for more residents to weigh in. For example, I collected more than 500 survey responses to inform a resolution I introduced and passed in support of funding for PKEEP. I also seek perspectives less formally through conversations with neighbors, parents, local organizations, businesses, and people using our public spaces.  I approach decisions by listening, educating myself about the issue, and trying not to enter with a predetermined answer. I consider resident input alongside available data, similar experiences and issues in other ANCs, agency expertise, and the broader impact on the District. Ultimately, I see my role as making informed decisions in the public interest, not tallying the loudest opinions or leaning on my perspective alone. I will explain how I reached a decision, be transparent about the factors I considered, and remain open to new information.
column37: I am the right person to continue serving 4C01 because I combine a deep personal investment in this neighborhood with a practical understanding of how to turn community concerns into action. That gives me direct knowledge of many of the systems I am working to improve—but I also know my experience is only one perspective. I have a responsibility to seek out and understand residents whose circumstances and relationships with the city differ from mine.  During my first term, I have built relationships with residents, schools, businesses, community organizations, fellow commissioners, and District agencies. I have learned when an issue calls for a formal resolution, when residents need a convener, and when progress depends on persistent behind-the-scenes follow-up.  I am responsive, curious, and willing to do the often unglamorous work of navigating city systems until residents get an answer. I would bring the knowledge and relationships I developed during my first term—along with the same openness, persistence, and commitment to making 4C01 work for everyone—to a second term.

column38: Yes. I believe our city should have a debate about using tax policy, in addition to zoning policy, to spur housing creation. For example, if an investor owns a parking lot on land zoned for high-density residential, they should be taxed as if they had built a high-density apartment building. I support affordable housing in every planning area, predictable development rules and more family-sized and homeownership opportunities. I also believe longtime residents must be protected from displacement and positioned to benefit from new investment.  Housing, transportation, public safety and economic development cannot be treated as separate conversations. My approach has been to connect them, move beyond individual projects and push for the level of coordinated investment our community deserves. In responding to the question about neighborhood character and the need for more housing, I chose to prioritize enabling more homes and more types of homes. However, I do not believe those goals have to be in conflict. Growth should respect the history, identity and character of our neighborhoods, and land-use regulations should guide building scale, design and transitions in ways that complement the surrounding community. Neighborhood character should help shape responsible growth, but it should not be used as a blanket justification for preventing new housing.

The term is also often used as shorthand for income-restricted affordable housing for low- and moderate-income households.  Market-rate housing is generally not income-restricted or subsidized, and its price is determined by the housing market. I do not think “affordable” simply means “cheap,” or that market-rate necessarily means “expensive.” A market-rate home can be affordable to a particular household depending on that household’s income, while an income-restricted unit can still be unaffordable to some households.  I think we need more housing across the spectrum, including both income-restricted affordable housing and market-rate housing. The proposed RFK development, which would add substantial new housing including affordable housing, is an important opportunity for the District and for Ward 7. Expanding our housing supply, while ensuring that new development includes meaningful affordable housing, is important to me.

I look forward to working as a Commissioner to make it easier for neighbors in ANC 1B and across DC to reduce their car use, both by supporting more transit, biking, and walking infrastructure, and by supporting bringing more housing, jobs, groceries and so forth within walking and biking distance of each other.
column35: While collecting signatures, I heard multiple times about the problems with rats in our rowhouse neighborhoods, and issues with trash collection that contribute to the pest problems. I have also heard from many residents that they have found it difficult or impossible to get through to our current Commissioner and to get responses from District staff. I look forward to working with fellow Commissioners and our colleagues across the Ward and around the District to push agencies to be more responsive to our constituents, and — mindful that we will also have several new Councilmembers and a new Mayor next year — to working with our Councilmembers to hold agency leaders responsible, find the systemic issues causing these problems, and create solutions and the oversight to ensure they are implemented, both during Performance Oversight/Budget in the spring and throughout the year.

column12: As an ANC 1E02 commissioner, I view affordable housing and market-rate housing as complementary parts of a healthy and inclusive neighborhood. Affordable housing is housing that is accessible to households with lower or moderate incomes, often through income-based requirements, public financing, or other affordability mechanisms. Market-rate housing, by contrast, is generally priced according to local market conditions, without income restrictions. The distinction is especially important in a neighborhood like ours, where rising housing costs can make it difficult for longtime residents, working families, seniors, and younger residents to remain in the community. While market-rate development can increase the overall housing supply and bring investment to the neighborhood, it does not necessarily create housing that is affordable to residents at every income level. I believe housing policy should support a range of housing types and price points while preserving the diversity and stability of our community. Increasing the supply of affordable housing alongside responsible market-rate development can help ensure that neighborhood growth benefits both current residents and future residents, rather than contributing to displacement or making the community accessible only to higher-income households.

column14: To me, family-sized housing means more than simply having multiple bedrooms. It means providing homes with enough space, privacy, and functionality for families to live comfortably as their needs change over time. This can include two- and three-bedroom apartments, townhomes, and other housing types that can accommodate parents, children, multigenerational households, or other family arrangements. Family-sized housing should also be genuinely attainable for working families—not limited to large units that are priced beyond the reach of most residents. In ANC 1E02, I believe we should encourage a range of housing options that allow families to remain in the neighborhood as they grow, while also supporting seniors, caregivers, and multigenerational households. A diverse housing stock strengthens a community. Families should have the opportunity to put down roots, children should be able to grow up near friends and schools, and residents should not have to leave the neighborhood simply because their household has grown. To me, creating and preserving family-sized housing is therefore both a housing issue and a community-stability issue.

column26: If 210 new homes needed to be built in ANC 1E02, I would concentrate the majority along the Georgia Avenue corridor, particularly around existing commercial and transit-accessible areas. I would look first at underused commercial properties, vacant lots, surface parking, and sites where redevelopment could add housing without displacing existing residents. Rather than putting all 210 homes on one site, I would favor several appropriately scaled projects along Georgia Avenue and at other major intersections. For example, redevelopment of underutilized commercial parcels could provide additional homes while also bringing new storefronts, services, and activity to the corridor. I would be less inclined to place significant new density in the middle of established residential blocks where it could create unnecessary displacement or conflicts with existing housing. I would also want the 210 homes to include a meaningful mix of affordable and market-rate units, including two- and three-bedroom homes for families. New development should be paired with improvements to sidewalks, pedestrian safety, transit access, public space, and other neighborhood infrastructure where needed. My basic approach would be: put more housing where there is already infrastructure and commercial activity, use underutilized land before displacing existing residents, and make sure new housing serves a range of incomes and household sizes. That would allow ANC 1E02 to add housing while strengthening rather than undermining the existing community.

column35: One of the biggest issues facing our neighborhood is rising housing costs and the risk of displacement. As prices increase, longtime residents, working families, seniors, and younger people may struggle to stay. At the same time, we need more housing to meet demand and ease pressure on supply.  My position is that ANC 1E02 should support responsible housing growth while prioritizing affordability, family-sized housing, and neighborhood stability. Development and affordability should go together. We can welcome new homes while advocating for affordable units, preserving existing affordable housing, and supporting housing for a range of households.  An ANC cannot set rents or directly control most housing policy, but commissioners can advocate and convene. If elected, I would engage residents early, communicate clearly about developments, and use the ANC to push for affordability, family-sized units, tenant protections, and community benefits.  I would also work with residents, housing groups, developers, and District agencies to support both new housing and preservation. Most importantly, I would ensure community concerns are consistently raised with decision-makers. My goal is to use the ANC’s voice to help shape growth so more residents can afford to stay in our neighborhood.
column36: I approach decision-making as an ANC commissioner by recognizing that I will never hear from every constituent directly, and that the voices I do hear may not reflect the full diversity of the neighborhood. Because of that, I would treat constituent input as one important source of information, not the only one.  To make balanced decisions, I would actively seek out a wide range of perspectives through office hours, community meetings, walking the neighborhood, surveys, and outreach to groups that are often less heard, including renters, seniors, young people, and non-English-speaking residents. I would also rely on data from District agencies, planning documents, and housing and demographic trends to understand the broader impact of issues affecting the community. My goal would be to combine lived experience with evidence, and to be transparent about how I reach conclusions.  I also recognize that ANC commissioners serve in an advisory role, which means part of my responsibility is to weigh competing interests and think about long-term neighborhood outcomes, not just immediate preferences. I would aim to make decisions that are fair, consistent, and grounded in equity, especially when different groups in the community have different needs or priorities.  Housing is a clear example of this. Rising housing costs and the risk of displacement affect many residents, but I would not assume there is a single community position on how to respond. Instead, I would listen to tenants concerned about affordability, homeowners concerned about neighborhood change, housing advocates focused on supply, and developers working within zoning constraints. I would then evaluate proposals based on how well they balance affordability, stability, and responsible growth.  In practice, I would use the ANC’s role to elevate community concerns to District agencies, encourage early and transparent engagement on development projects, and advocate for outcomes that expand housing options while protecting long-term residents. My decisions would be guided by a commitment to represent the whole community as fairly as possible, even when not every voice can be heard equally or agree.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as an ANC commissioner because I would bring a thoughtful, inclusive, and practical approach to representing my SMD. I understand that the role is not simply to represent the loudest voices, but to listen to residents with different experiences and priorities and work toward solutions that serve the broader community.  I would make myself accessible through community meetings, office hours, neighborhood walks, and direct outreach, while making a deliberate effort to hear from renters, homeowners, seniors, families, young people, and residents who may not typically participate in ANC meetings.  I also believe good representation requires more than listening. I would review the facts, understand District policies and data, seek out different perspectives, and be transparent about how I reach decisions. On issues such as housing, development, transportation, public safety, and neighborhood services, I would balance immediate concerns with the long-term interests of the community.  I recognize the ANC's authority is limited, but I believe commissioners can be effective advocates. I would elevate constituent concerns to the appropriate agencies, engage early on important proposals, build constructive relationships, and follow through.  Most importantly, I would work to represent the entire SMD fairly and consistently. My goal is to be accessible, prepared, respectful, and accountable to the community I serve.
column38: I would like GGWash to understand that my positions on housing, affordable housing, transportation, and land use are fundamentally connected. I believe ANC 1E02 should be a neighborhood where people at different income levels and stages of life can afford to live, where families can find appropriately sized homes, and where residents can access jobs, schools, businesses, parks, and services without being dependent on a car. I support adding housing, particularly along major corridors such as Georgia Avenue and on vacant or underutilized commercial properties, surface parking lots, and other sites where additional density can be accommodated responsibly. I believe increasing the housing supply is important, but I do not view housing as simply a numbers exercise. New development should include affordable and family-sized housing and should be planned with the needs of existing residents in mind. Affordable housing should also mean preserving affordability that already exists. I would support efforts to prevent displacement and preserve existing affordable homes, while recognizing that the District needs to build substantially more housing to meet current and future demand. We should be able to pursue both goals at the same time. Transportation and land use should be planned together. I support making it easier and safer to walk, bike, and use public transportation, particularly along corridors where we are encouraging additional housing. New development should be accompanied by attention to pedestrian safety, sidewalks, transit access, traffic impacts, and public infrastructure. Finally, I recognize the limits of the ANC's authority. I would not promise residents that an ANC can solve the District's housing or transportation challenges by itself. Instead, I would focus on using the Commission's voice effectively: engaging residents early, reviewing proposals carefully, advocating with District agencies, and building constructive relationships with community organizations, planners, developers, and other stakeholders. My goal is a neighborhood that grows without losing its diversity—a place where new residents are welcomed, longtime residents can stay, and public investment and development work together to create a more affordable, connected, and resilient community.

column26: Although ANC 2B is already the fifth most densely populated ANC, there are still opportunities to add hundreds more housing units. The Safeway, the McDonalds and the CVS on 17th St are low density commercial sites on prime corner lots in a major corridor. I would like to see these sites developed for mixed residential and retail use as long as it can be done, in the case of Safeway and CVS, while maintaining those retail businesses on the ground level after construction. Just those three underutilized lots could support possibly hundreds of new homes. Although just outside ANC 2B, I strongly support the proposed development of the police/fire station at 1617 U and would like to see the re-zoning issue reopened so that the entire block is up-zoned. Upzoning the entire block would allow an additional 175 units to be built and it’s possible that this could be accomplished through changes to the Comprehensive Plan which is currently under review. Furthermore, with the election of Janeese Lewis-George as Mayor, there is an opportunity for this site to be used for social housing rather than the usual private sector mix of market rate and affordable units. Also just outside ANC 2B is the Sunoco station currently being demolished at 15th and U which would be a prime location to build hundreds of units of new housing. There is no information available about what the owner’s plans are for that site, but ensuring that as much new housing as possible is built on that site should be a priority. Finally, there are a few other lots actually in ANC 2B that could be ripe for residential development: the Shell station on 18th St, the surface parking lot at 1919 Massachusetts Ave (with the Connecticut Avenue deckover, no longer critical for the Dupont Circle farmer's market) and the parking lot for St. Luke's on Church St. There should be incentives for converting surface parking to residential development, just as there are for office conversions.

column35: The biggest issue for my SMD is traffic safety. The future of 17th St between R and P is a key piece: the protected bike lanes north of R and south of P have slowed traffic and made the street safer. But between R and P, compromises made to preserve streateries left a bike lane going north with none going south, while the pre-existing delivery truck problem was never addressed. I support pedestrianizing 17th St between R and P provided alley access for residents and trash/recycling collection is preserved. But even if that’s only possible in the longer term, more can be done now: with the streateries on the west side gone, a two-way protected bike lane there should be revisited. The ANC should also work with Safeway, True Value, CVS and other businesses to end 53-ft trailer deliveries and restrict delivery hours — at peak times, trucks routinely block crosswalks, a problem that predates the bike lanes. All flex posts should become permanent curb extensions; trucks and cars currently drive over them, endangering pedestrians and cyclists. I support protected bike lanes on Q and R Streets even if it costs a lane of parking, though a two-way lane on R St alone (rather than one-way lanes on both streets) may better preserve parking. Finally, as the protected bike network expands, I support extending the downtown prohibition on riding bicycles and personal mobility devices on sidewalks to ANC 2B. Our often-narrow sidewalks should primarily be for pedestrians.  If elected, I would introduce a resolution asking the DC Council and DDOT to extend to ANC 2B the existing prohibition on riding bicycles and personal mobility devices on sidewalks in the Central Business District. As the protected bike network expands, I believe sidewalks in ANC 2B should primarily be for pedestrians. Many are narrow and already heavily used, and pedestrians should not have to compete with bikes and scooters for limited space. The ANC should also work with DDOT to identify locations where better bike infrastructure can make this restriction practical while preserving safe routes for cyclists.
column36: First, ANC members have to follow established law and procedures as they currently stand, not as they wish them to be. For example, if 60% of the property owners on a block follow the established procedure and petition to replace a female gingko tree with a male tree, the ANC should consider that petition on its merits. Blocking it or, worse, refusing even to consider it without a specific reason, simply because the ANC members oppose ever replacing a healthy mature tree, is an abuse of their discretionary power. Second, although it won't be possible to hear from all constituents, it's important for ANC members to solicit feedback from their constituents and keep their constituents informed of important matters that directly affect their SMDs. I intend to do both. I will try to listen respectfully to constituents who wish to make their views known to me. And even if I have a strongly held view on a matter, that doesn't mean that concerns expressed by individual constituents should just be dismissed out of hand. For example, I strongly support the bike lanes and road diet that have transformed 17th Street between Massachusetts Avenue and T St. But I know there are residents of my SMD who have serious concerns, particularly about pedestrian safety. To the extent those concerns can be reasonably addressed, they should be. At the same time, I would not give undue weight to the views of various civic associations that are unlikely to represent the views of the majority of residents in my SMD. Finally, it's important to recognize that, although ANCs are hyperlocal bodies, the vast majority of ANC members run unopposed and, even in those cases where there is more than one candidate, most voters are not well informed about the views of the candidates. For this reason, a little humility is in order. I think that ANCs should largely stick to weighing in on local matters that directly affect their constituents rather than treating every citywide policy debate as an occasion for a resolution — whether the topic is land use, historic preservation or something else entirely. There's a difference between taking the job seriously and taking yourself seriously. If elected to ANC 2B, I intend to do the former and try to avoid too much of the latter.

column12: Affordable housing in ANC 4B06 generally refers to units that are means-tested, income‑restricted, subsidized, or rent‑controlled, ensuring residents pay no more than 30% of their household income on housing costs, aligning with federal definitions and local interpretations. These units are often created through programs like Inclusionary Zoning, which requires developers of larger residential projects to set aside a percentage of units as affordable, tying the number of units to building size so that increased density can produce more affordable homes. Market‑rate housing, by contrast, is built by private developers without subsidies or rent controls and is typically more expensive, often costing more than 30% of a household’s income and reflecting prevailing real‑estate market conditions rather than an affordability standard. In ANC 4B06, the distinction matters because the community’s housing strategy emphasizes adding density near transit corridors to expand supply while ensuring affordability is preserved through income‑restricted units. Affordable housing supports lower‑income residents by capping costs and providing long‑term stability, while market‑rate housing expands overall inventory but does not inherently meet affordability needs unless paired with policy tools requiring set‑asides or deeper affordability levels.

column35: Our streets were not designed for the level of vehicle speed and volume they experience today, and the result is an environment where near‑misses, unsafe crossings, and resident complaints have become routine. Too many intersections lack all‑way stop control and too many pedestrian crossings rely on faded paint or insufficient signage to keep people safe. I believe that safe, walkable streets are a fundamental neighborhood right, not an amenity, and that building this environment starts with strong advocacy, thoughtful data collection, and persistent follow‑through with District agencies. I would push for targeted DDOT evaluations at the most hazardous intersections and request the installation of four‑way stop signs, speed humps, raised crosswalks, and upgraded pedestrian signageBy combining constituent input with agency partnership and evidence‑based solutions, I would work to create calmer, safer streets that support walking, biking, and everyday neighborhood life.  If elected, I would focus on addressing what I believe is the neighborhood’s biggest issue: traffic safety. Unsafe intersections, frequent speeding, and inadequate pedestrian protections continue to put residents—especially children, seniors, and people with disabilities—at risk, and improving street safety is both urgent and achievable within an ANC commissioner’s authority. My strategy would begin with systematically identifying the most dangerous intersections and corridors through community feedback, walk audits, and data shared by DDOT. I would then file formal ANC resolutions requesting all‑way stop conversions, speed humps, raised crosswalks, clearer signage, and curb extensions, prioritizing locations where residents report near‑misses or where previous incident data shows heightened risk. Because the ANC’s power is advisory, I would maintain regular communication with DDOT to ensure requests are not only logged but advanced through the evaluation and installation process. By combining evidence‑based advocacy, structured community engagement, and consistent agency coordination, I would work to create safer, calmer, and more walkable streets for everyone in our neighborhood.

column12: At its core, the distinction between affordable housing and market-rate housing lies in how rents are set, who the homes serve, and the funding mechanisms behind them.  Market-Rate Housing  Market-rate housing operates on private market supply and demand dynamics. Rents and sale prices are set by property owners to maximize revenue based on location, amenities, and market competition. While market-rate supply is essential for absorbing overall demand and reducing broad regional price pressures, market forces alone do not set prices low enough to accommodate lower-income households without consuming an unsustainable portion of their earnings.  Affordable Housing  Affordable housing is structurally protected so that housing costs do not exceed 30% of a household's gross income. It encompasses two primary forms:  Income-Restricted / Subsidized Affordable Housing: Capped by government regulations, tax credits (like LIHTC), local subsidies (like DC's Housing Production Trust Fund), or Inclusionary Zoning (IZ). Eligibility is tied to specific Area Median Income (AMI) bands—such as 30%, 50%, or 80% AMI—ensuring homes remain accessible to low- and moderate-income working families, seniors, and service workers.  Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH): Older, un-subsidized private market properties that remain affordable due to age or location.  Both market-rate and affordable housing are necessary components of a balanced, equitable city housing ecosystem.

We must aggressively hold absentee property owners accountable, turn blighted lots into high-quality housing, and redesign our streetscapes to prioritize pedestrian, bus, and micro-mobility safety over dangerous vehicle speeds.  Given the advisory nature of an ANC Commissioner’s authority, I will realistically work within statutory mechanisms to deliver concrete outcomes:  Leverage Great Weight Oversight: Draft and pass formal ANC resolutions targeting problematic properties, urging DOB and OAG to enforce tax penalties, secure vacant structures, or pursue judicial receivership for affordable housing.  Coordinate Targeted Municipal Audits: Organize structured multi-agency site walkthroughs (with DPW, DOB, and MPD) to log code violations, audit 311 service tickets, and clear dumping hot spots.  Push DDOT Traffic Safety Input: Submit resolutions advocating for tactical traffic-calming measures to protect residents walking to transit and neighborhood schools.
column36: As an ANC Commissioner representing Single Member District 8A01, making fair, effective decisions requires balancing constituent feedback with rigorous policy analysis, proactive outreach, and data-driven equity. Relying solely on inbox messages or evening meetings risks favoring a vocal minority over working families, renters, seniors, and youth who lack time to attend multi-hour public forums.  To serve the entire community, I guide my leadership through a four-part framework:  1. Proactive Community Engagement  Instead of waiting for residents to reach out, I meet them where they gather. I conduct regular neighborhood walkthroughs, hold pop-up office hours at parks and bus stops, maintain an active digital presence, and collaborate with local schools, churches, and tenant associations to gather broad, representative input.  2. Grounding Decisions in Data & Policy  I weigh constituent feedback against land-use data, traffic safety metrics, housing production numbers, and long-range city plans. Decisions shouldn't stem from loud pushback alone; they must be grounded in evidence showing long-term benefits for affordability, safety, and neighborhood quality of life.  3. Applying an Equity & Anti-Displacement Lens  Land-use and transit decisions in Ward 8 carry high stakes for affordability and equity. I evaluate every proposal by asking: Who benefits, and who bears the cost? I prioritize keeping long-term residents housed, attracting essential commercial services, protecting vulnerable road users, and expanding housing choices.  4. Transparent Communication  On contentious issues, I clearly explain the rationale behind my votes. Through published meeting summaries and updates, I detail the data, statutory context, and public input that shaped each decision.  Ultimately, my role is to act as an accessible, accountable trustee—using proactive outreach, data analysis, and equity-focused policy to build a safer, more vibrant neighborhood for all 2,000 constituents.

I understand both the administrative tools available to an ANC—such as leveraging statutory "great weight" on zoning and land-use decisions—and the essential work of partnering directly with agencies like DPW, DOB, and DDOT to deliver everyday results for residents.  Having managed community projects, public communications, and local outreach, I prioritize transparent, data-grounded decision-making that puts equity, housing access, and anti-displacement at the forefront. column38: In Ward 8 and across Single Member District 8A01, housing, land use, and transportation are not isolated policy silos—they are deeply interconnected drivers of equity, displacement prevention, and community health. When considering my positions, I encourage Greater Greater Washington (GGWash) to keep three core principles at the center:  1. Equity Means Proactive Investment East of the River  For too long, policy debates in the District have treated housing production and infrastructure investments as one-size-fits-all across every Ward. While Ward 3 needs aggressive upzoning to unlock high-opportunity areas, Ward 8 requires a balanced strategy that pairs density and missing-middle housing with strict anti-displacement protections, tenant support, and capital investments in long-neglected commercial corridors. We must legalize rowhomes, triplexes, and sixplexes while ensuring that public land disposition, Inclusionary Zoning, and Housing Production Trust Fund resources deliver deeply affordable, family-sized units directly where working families are at risk of being priced out.  2. Complete Streets and Transit Reliability Are Civil Rights Issues  In Historic Anacostia and Fairlawn, a significant portion of our residents rely on Metrobus and walking to reach jobs, healthcare, and schools. Yet, our corridors continue to suffer from speed-heavy vehicle traffic, delayed buses, and unsafe pedestrian crossings. Transportation policy must explicitly prioritize vulnerable road users over private automobile throughput. Dedicated bus lanes, protected micro-mobility infrastructure, and automated traffic enforcement along corridors like Good Hope Road SE and Marion Barry Avenue SE are essential tools to save lives, improve bus transit speeds, and connect East of the River residents to regional economic opportunities.  3. Activating Blighted and Vacant Land First  Before expanding development into established residential green spaces, our immediate land-use focus should be turning tax-delinquent, vacant, and blighted structures into active housing and community assets. Neglected parcels drag down local safety, encourage illegal dumping, and hold back neighborhood vitality. By streamlining District agency oversight—pushing DOB, OAG, and DMPED to utilize judicial receivership, tax auctions, and public land transfers—we can rapidly convert neighborhood eyesores into vibrant market-rate and income-restricted housing.  Ultimately, my goal as an ANC Commissioner is to bring a forward-thinking, multimodal, and supply-positive urbanism to Ward 8—one that embraces density, insists on transit equity, and protects the long-term culture and residents of our community.

column12: Affordable housing and market-rate housing serve different purposes within the overall housing market, but both are essential to creating healthy, economically diverse communities. Affordable housing is designed to ensure that households can obtain safe, decent housing without spending more than approximately 30 percent of their income on housing costs. It may be income-restricted, subsidized, or developed through public-private partnerships, although not all affordable housing receives direct government subsidies.  Market-rate housing is priced according to current market conditions and is generally not income-restricted or subsidized. Rental rates and home prices are determined by supply and demand rather than affordability requirements. Depending on a household's income, market-rate housing may be affordable for some residents but unaffordable for others.  A balanced housing strategy should include a range of housing options—including affordable, workforce, and market-rate housing—to meet the needs of individuals and families at different income levels. Expanding the housing supply, encouraging mixed-income developments, streamlining development processes, and fostering public-private partnerships can help improve housing affordability while supporting economic growth, neighborhood stability, and a high quality of life for all residents.

column12: Affordable housing should mean more than simply labeling a unit “affordable.” It should mean that working people and families can pay their rent without having to choose between housing, groceries, health care, or transportation. That often requires income restrictions, public investment, rent limits, or other protections that keep homes within reach over time. Market-rate housing is different because its price is largely driven by the market and is not required to serve people at a particular income level. We need more housing overall, including market-rate housing, but increasing supply alone will not meet every need. Public investment and long-term affordability protections are still necessary to make sure lower-income residents are not priced out. The real distinction is whether there is a meaningful and enforceable commitment to keeping the housing affordable for the people who need it most.
